EGS could be commercialized by 2030, with a projected national average cost of $60–$70 per MWh by 2030, and potentially $40–$50 per MWh in select regions (DOE EERE 2023). The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Enhanced Geothermal Shot is aiming to reduce costs to $45 per MWh by 2035. According to an NLR expert, several CLG systems have been demonstrated globally. Risks associated with inaccurate resource characterization and site identification are lower for next-generation geothermal than traditional geothermal (DOE EERE 2023). According to an NLR expert, technical challenges can include creating sufficient area for heat transfer in the surrounding rock. Overall, the high initial investment in project development could present the greatest hurdle in using advanced geothermal technologies. E.3 Power Beaming Optical and radio frequency power-beaming technologies enable the wireless transfer of power to remote areas and allow for power generation to occur in different areas from power use. Electricity is generated at one point, such as using solar PV panels or a generator, and then transmitted using laser beams to the site where the electricity will be used. The transmission can occur through air as land-to-land and land-to-air (to UAVs), through space as satellite-to-satellite and space-to-ground (radio frequency), or through fiber-optic cables (including powering tethered UAVs). Advantages of the technology include reducing some supply chain complexities by removing the need to mobilize energy generation equipment, such as solar PV infrastructure, or transport fuels. Power beaming offers more reliable energy availability by transmitting power to areas that might be less suitable for traditional DERs, including solar PV. This technology can be adapted for directed energy weapons, similar to how nuclear technology serves both civilian and military purposes. As advancements are made in directed energy weapon systems, progress in these areas could accelerate developments in power-beaming technologies and vice versa, potentially enhancing both military capabilities and broader energy applications. According to NLR experts, the use of high-energy laser beams creates a safety risk, and the lack of extensive field-testing creates uncertainty regarding field performance. Adversarial threats include possible power interception and cybersecurity threats. Although laser and radio frequency power conversion technologies are commercially available, other technological challenges need to be resolved before wireless power beaming can be commercialized. These hurdles include system integration issues and thermal dissipation at the receiving point as a limitation on the amount of power that can be transferred.
